paragraphs: This paper develops a radial basis function classifier that grows where distinguishing classes is difficult. RBF centers provide local responses to inputs. Instead of distributing additional centers throughout the data, the boundary hunting method places them near class boundaries, concentrating its representational resources on regions where classification errors arise.

The classifier adds complexity where examples are confused and the relevant RBF outputs are similar. A predicted squared error measure controls both how many centers to introduce and when construction should stop. This makes network growth part of learning, with an explicit criterion for deciding whether more local detail is useful.

The authors test the method on artificial two-class data and a seismic database with seven classes and 14 features. The artificial example includes several clusters per class but concentrates boundary difficulty in only one cluster. In both experiments, the method reports lower error with fewer centers than conventional RBF, Gaussian mixture, or multilayer perceptron classifiers. The findings support allocating complexity according to classification difficulty.
neurips-1992-a-boundary-hunting-radial-b.tldr: A growing RBF classifier concentrates centers near confusing class boundaries, achieving lower error with fewer centers in two experiments.

paragraphs: In high-speed communication, neighboring transmitted symbols can interfere with one another, making the received signal difficult to interpret. Channel equalization addresses this distortion. The paper questions the usual framing of equalization as reversing the channel, because a smaller residual error after inversion does not directly establish a lower probability of choosing the wrong symbol.

The authors instead formulate equalization as classification: the equalizer must decide which symbol produced the observation. They describe the optimal classifier through the Bayes decision rule. This changes the focus from how accurately a transformation reverses distortion to how accurately the resulting system distinguishes the possible transmitted symbols.

Because the optimal decision rule is generally nonlinear, the paper proposes an efficient training approach combining linear and nonlinear components. On an experimental channel, this hybrid equalizer has a lower error probability than a linear equalizer. The result supports the classification formulation in that setting and shows why nonlinear decision making can help with the actual communication objective.
neurips-1992-a-hybrid-linear-nonlinear-a.tldr: Treating channel equalization as symbol classification motivates a hybrid equalizer that beats a linear equalizer on an experimental channel.

paragraphs: Trajectory Extension Learning teaches robot control through a sequence of progressively harder movements. Its central assumption is that some parameter of the desired trajectory can vary smoothly from an easily controlled regime to the target behavior. This supplies a route through intermediate tasks instead of requiring the robot to master difficult dynamics immediately.

As that parameter changes gradually, a neural network learns the robot's inverse dynamics: the relationship needed to obtain motor commands for a desired movement. The practice movements remain near the intended path while learning proceeds. Average speed provides the paper's example, allowing learning to begin with simpler slow movements and extend toward faster ones.

The paper demonstrates the idea on a real two-joint direct-drive robot arm. Its broader contribution is the notion of a practice strategy, where choosing the order of tasks helps make a complex control problem learnable. The smoothly adjustable trajectory parameter is essential to this particular strategy because it connects the manageable starting behavior to the desired behavior.
neurips-1992-a-practice-strategy-for-rob.tldr: A robot learns difficult movements by gradually extending easier practice trajectories while a neural network learns inverse dynamics.

paragraphs: SESAME is a software framework for designing, simulating, and analyzing neural networks. The paper treats the simulator as an important part of research practice: as experiments become more complex, researchers need tools that make their models understandable and manageable. Its design aims to follow the way researchers naturally describe computational models.

Experiments are assembled as networks of extensible building blocks. This organization makes the components of a model explicit and provides a way to introduce new components as research needs change. The framework's flexibility therefore comes from how experiments are represented, as well as from the mechanisms available for constructing them.

Those mechanisms include automatic configuration of building blocks for a particular experiment and multiple inheritance at runtime. The latter allows components to combine inherited behavior while the system is running. Together, these features are intended to support the construction and analysis of complicated architectures. The contribution is a framework for organizing neural-network experimentation, with transparency, manageability, and extensibility as its central design goals.
neurips-1992-an-object-oriented-framewor.tldr: SESAME organizes neural-network experiments as extensible building blocks to make complex models easier to construct, inspect, and manage.

paragraphs: This paper explores how an analog model of the cochlea can represent speech. Its starting point is the tension between identifying frequencies precisely and locating rapid changes in time. That tension is particularly important for broadband signals, which contain multiple frequency components and can change too quickly for a single fixed analysis resolution to capture everything clearly.

The model produces a response resembling wavelet analysis across scales while retaining good temporal resolution. It also carries frequency information in the timing of its auditory-fiber responses. Specifically, the intervals between peaks in instantaneous firing rates allow the frequencies of individual components in a broadband signal to be determined accurately.

The authors demonstrate these properties using natural speech and synthetic complex signals. The significance is that frequency information need not be read only from a conventional spectral display: response timing also provides useful structure. The cochlear model combines analysis across scales with a temporal code, offering a way to describe rapidly changing speech while preserving information about its constituent frequencies.
neurips-1992-analog-cochlear-model-for-m.tldr: An analog cochlear model combines wavelet-like analysis with response timing to preserve rapid changes and identify frequencies in speech.

paragraphs: This paper implements a method for estimating gradients and performing gradient descent directly in analog VLSI hardware. The target is a scalar function computed on the chip, whose value depends on several adjustable parameters. Optimization requires estimating how changes in those parameters affect the function and then moving toward settings that reduce it.

The circuit estimates derivatives by injecting noise and using multiplicative correlation. The perturbations reveal how the measured function responds to parameter changes, providing the directional information needed for descent. This makes gradient estimation itself part of the on-chip computation and supports continuous adjustment across multiple dimensions.

One intended use is automatic circuit tuning, replacing manual parameter setting. Another is adjusting synaptic weights for an on-chip learning system, including a backpropagation implementation. The authors present measurements from the analog hardware and describe the possibility of annealing-style optimization alongside continuous gradient descent. The contribution is a physical implementation of an optimization mechanism that could serve both circuit calibration and learning.
neurips-1992-analog-vlsi-implementation-.tldr: An analog chip uses injected noise and correlation to estimate gradients for automatic parameter tuning and potential on-chip learning.

paragraphs: The paper studies associative neural networks with local inhibition, where inhibitory interactions shape how activity develops. It reports improved computational performance relative to classical Hopfield-like networks. Two specific benefits are increased critical storage capacity and a greater ability to store correlated patterns, which share structure rather than being entirely distinct.

The network's dynamics also provide information about memory overload. When too much is stored, the devices exhibit chaotic behavior with exponentially long transients. A transient is the period before the system settles into its eventual behavior, so prolonged unsettled activity becomes an indicator that the associative memory has exceeded its useful loading regime.

The authors connect this analysis to a programmable hardware implementation containing 16 neurons. A major feature is reconfigurability: weights, transfer functions, or even the architecture can be changed by downloading a new configuration to the chip. The work therefore combines a claim about improved memory behavior with a concrete implementation that supports modifying the network design through software.
neurips-1992-attractor-neural-networks-w.tldr: Local inhibition improves associative-memory capacity and correlated-pattern storage, with the design demonstrated in a reconfigurable 16-neuron circuit.

paragraphs: This paper recognizes letters spoken continuously, a task with relatively few possible labels but substantial confusion between them. Its Multi-State Time Delay Neural Network combines a time-delay network's ability to identify speech sounds with dynamic time warping. The alignment procedure accommodates timing differences while the complete system performs word-level classification and learns through backpropagation.

The reported word accuracies are 98.5% for speaker-dependent recognition and 92.0% for speaker-independent recognition. These results exceed previously reported performance on the same databases. The distinction matters because recognizing a familiar speaker and handling speakers independently are different recognition settings, and the paper reports them separately.

The authors also propose training changes aimed at whole-sentence performance. These include allowing alignment across word boundaries, modeling word duration, and propagating errors from the sentence level rather than only individual words. Architectures with submodules specialized for subsets of speakers yield further improvements. Together, these directions connect local sound recognition, sequence alignment, and speaker variation within one trainable recognition architecture.
neurips-1992-connected-letter-recognitio.tldr: An MS-TDNN combines learned speech features and flexible alignment to recognize continuously spoken letters with strong reported accuracy.

paragraphs: This paper asks what kinds of filters emerge when a processing stage is optimized to preserve information about its inputs. It uses infomax, which maximizes average mutual information between input and output while accounting for constraints and processing noise. The investigation applies this principle to a class of nonlinear mappings.

Under certain conditions, the resulting filters have several useful properties. For an individual input, activity tends to concentrate in a relatively small number of output nodes. The filters also respond to statistical structure beyond pairwise correlations. When the input features are localized, their receptive fields—the portions of the input to which they respond—also tend to become localized.

For some input ensembles, favored solutions include filters operating at multiple resolutions, with subsampling at low spatial frequencies. These solutions are related to pyramid and wavelet representations. The significance is that sparse activity, localized sensitivity, and multiresolution structure can arise from a common encoding objective. The stated conditions and dependence on input statistics are central to what the result establishes.
neurips-1992-deriving-receptive-fields-u.tldr: Under suitable conditions, maximizing information preservation produces sparse responses, localized receptive fields, and multiresolution filters.

paragraphs: The paper examines model selection during training, before a neural network has converged. Its starting point is stopped training: train an oversized network, monitor its error on a separate validation set, and stop when that error deteriorates. This makes the course of training itself part of choosing an effective model.

The authors extend this approach by allowing the network's complexity to change during learning. One extension dynamically prunes weights, modifying the network's topology as training proceeds. Another adjusts the weight of a complexity penalty over time, changing how strongly the learning process discourages complexity at different stages.

The paper reports that these extensions can significantly improve the performance of stopped training. Their importance lies in coordinating several decisions that are otherwise easy to treat separately: how long to train, which connections to retain, and how strongly to penalize complexity. Model selection becomes a process carried out along the training trajectory, with no requirement that each candidate network first reach a converged solution.
neurips-1992-extended-regularization-met.tldr: Dynamic weight pruning and changing complexity penalties improve model selection performed before neural-network training converges.

paragraphs: The EPSILON paper presents an analog neural-processing chip built using CMOS VLSI technology. The device was both designed and fabricated, making the contribution a working hardware implementation. Its purpose is to carry out neural computation through a physical circuit, with the chip's measured operation forming a central part of the work.

The chip represents neural states using streams of pulses. These signals provide the means by which neural activity is communicated within the device. The reported processing capability is approximately 360 million synaptic connections per second. That figure describes the rate of synaptic computation, giving a concrete measure of the hardware's computational throughput.

The paper also includes basic characterization results and demonstrates the chip on real-world problems. These address complementary questions: characterization establishes how the fabricated device operates, while application demonstrations show it being used for problem solving. The stated contribution therefore joins a particular signaling approach, a measured processing rate, and demonstrations of neural computation in functioning analog hardware.
neurips-1992-generic-analog-neural-compu.tldr: The fabricated EPSILON analog neural chip uses pulse-stream signaling and processes about 360 million synaptic connections per second.

paragraphs: Neuronal responses in cat and monkey visual cortex can alternate between apparently coordinated oscillations and more stochastic activity. This paper investigates whether those episodes reflect switching between underlying collective states. It develops two complementary descriptions: one inferred from recorded spike trains and another derived from a model of interacting spiking neurons.

The data-based approach uses a hidden state model whose parameters describe network dynamics and individual neurons' coupling to the network. Applied to multi-unit recordings from cat visual cortex, it supports the presence of oscillatory and stochastic states and quantifies transitions between them. This turns visible changes in spike activity into an analysis of hidden assembly behavior.

The microscopic approach represents the assembly through a phase density and derives an equation for its evolution. With nonlinear synaptic interactions, a limit cycle and a fixed point can coexist as attractors, and external fluctuations can trigger switching. The authors show consistency between the two approaches, linking the inferred states to a possible dynamical mechanism for the observed temporal structure.
neurips-1992-how-oscillatory-neuronal-re.tldr: Two consistent models explain alternating cortical activity as fluctuation-driven switching between coexisting collective states.

paragraphs: This paper applies boosting to handwritten character recognition by constructing an ensemble of learning machines. The motivating theory can turn a learner with error below 50% into one with arbitrarily low error, but the algorithm considered requires many independent training samples. The authors describe a way around that sampling obstacle for their recognition experiments.

They evaluate boosting on four handwritten datasets: 12,000 USPS digits from segmented ZIP codes, along with NIST collections containing 220,000 digits, 45,000 uppercase letters, and 45,000 lowercase letters. This examines the approach across both digit and alphabet recognition, rather than drawing its conclusion from one character collection.

Performance is assessed through overall error when every pattern receives a decision and through the rejection rate needed to keep errors among accepted patterns at 1%. The latter captures how much input the system must decline to classify to reach a chosen accuracy. Boosting substantially improves performance over a single network, with improvements reaching a factor of three in some cases.
neurips-1992-improving-performance-in-ne.tldr: Boosted neural-network ensembles improve handwritten character recognition, with gains reaching a factor of three in some cases.

paragraphs: Input Reconstruction Reliability Estimation evaluates how dependable a neural network's response is by examining its internal representation. The method applies to a restricted class of multilayer perceptrons. Its central idea is that a network's ability to preserve information about the current input can serve as evidence about the reliability of its response.

The technique reconstructs the input pattern from that internal representation and assesses how accurately the reconstruction matches the original. Better reconstruction is interpreted as greater reliability. This makes the estimate sensitive to the particular input being processed: it asks how well the network represents that pattern, rather than assigning one reliability level to the network as a whole.

The paper reports useful reliability estimates for networks trained for autonomous driving. It also presents results using those estimates to choose among networks trained for different driving situations. The practical contribution is therefore both an assessment method and a way to guide network selection, using reconstruction quality as the signal for deciding which trained network to rely on.
neurips-1992-input-reconstruction-reliab.tldr: Input reconstruction quality estimates response reliability and helps select among neural networks trained for different driving situations.

paragraphs: This paper studies how neural-network performance changes as the number of training examples grows. It distinguishes two learning curves: training loss, measured on the examples used for fitting, and predictive or generalization loss, which concerns predictions beyond those examples. Comparing these curves connects learning from a finite sample with the network's complexity.

The analysis clarifies their asymptotic properties and their relationship. Asymptotic behavior concerns what happens as the amount of training data becomes large. Examining both curves together gives a way to understand how the network's fit to its training examples relates to its predictive performance as more evidence becomes available.

The resulting theory provides a natural definition of neural-network complexity and a new model-selection criterion. The significance is that complexity is linked to learning behavior, giving the choice of a model a basis in the relationship between fitting and prediction. The contribution is therefore a theoretical connection among sample size, the two kinds of loss, and the selection of a suitable network.
neurips-1992-learning-curves-model-selec.tldr: An asymptotic analysis of training and predictive learning curves yields a definition of network complexity and a model-selection criterion.

paragraphs: An object's appearance can change over time while its identity remains the same. This paper uses that persistence as a learning signal for categorization. Rather than supplying category labels, it lets a feed-forward network observe trajectories of changing patterns and learn from the relationship between neighboring observations.

The learning procedure maximizes mutual information between the network's representations at consecutive time steps. Mutual information measures how informative one representation is about the next. The objective therefore encourages the network to discover structure that carries across successive appearances, using temporal relationships to help organize its representation of the observed patterns.

The authors demonstrate entirely unsupervised classification of an ensemble of several patterns. The observed sequences include abrupt changes from one object to another between trajectories, so the demonstration does not require every neighboring observation to belong to the same object. The result supports temporal coherence as a useful cue for learning categories. The authors also suggest that the procedure could apply to other perceptual learning tasks.
neurips-1992-learning-to-categorize-obje.tldr: A network learns categories without labels by maximizing information shared between representations of consecutive observations.

paragraphs: Saccade combines locating handwritten characters with recognizing them. A single network learns to classify the character centered in its input window and estimate the distances from the window's center to the current and next characters. Recognition and movement guidance are therefore learned together as parts of reading a line.

During testing, the system uses those classifications and distance estimates with jumping rules to move between characters. The design draws on large and corrective eye movements: the system moves toward an informative location and uses positioning information to guide its progress. The network learns distance estimates despite differences in character width, spacing, writing style, and other factors.

The paper reports accurate and efficient recognition of handwritten digits and describes locating characters whether they touch or remain separate. This matters because identifying character boundaries and interpreting characters are closely connected tasks. Saccade makes the classifier contribute directly to navigation, allowing its learned view of the text to help determine where the system should look next.
neurips-1992-learning-to-see-where-and-w.tldr: Saccade trains one network to recognize handwritten characters and guide jumps along a line using learned position estimates.

paragraphs: The paper addresses how a network can acquire an appropriate number of adjustable parameters during learning. Constructive algorithms do this by adding hidden units. Metamorphosis algorithms explore a different possibility: keep the number of units fixed while gradually increasing the number of parameters that can vary freely.

The investigated architecture places radial basis function units on a lattice. This arrangement imposes flexible constraints on network parameters. Changing the constraints changes how much freedom the existing units have, so the model can become more expressive without increasing its unit count. The distinction between the number of units and the number of independent parameters is the key idea.

The authors identify benefits including variable subset selection, robust parameter selection, processing at multiple resolutions, and interpolation from sparse training data. These connect controlled flexibility to several aspects of learning: which inputs matter, how parameters are chosen, and how finely the data are represented. The approach frames model growth as a gradual release of constraints within an existing architecture.
neurips-1992-metamorphosis-networks-an-a.tldr: Metamorphosis networks increase learning capacity by relaxing parameter constraints while keeping the number of units fixed.

paragraphs: This paper investigates whether a speech recognizer can use speaker-related consistency while retaining a largely speaker-independent model. It focuses on gender as the conditioning variable. The proposed Gender Dependent Neural Network can be tuned for each gender while sharing most of its parameters across speakers, combining specialization with a common recognition model.

A classification network helps generate gender-dependent probabilities for speech sounds. These probabilities feed a statistical recognizer based on a hidden Markov model, making the method part of a hybrid neural-network and HMM system. The intended benefit is to incorporate a persistent speaker characteristic into the probabilities used for recognizing continuous speech.

The gender classifier achieves 98.3% accuracy on a Resource Management test set. However, integrating the gender-dependent network produces a recognition-score improvement that is not statistically significant on that test set. The findings separate two outcomes: the system can predict the conditioning category accurately, but that success does not establish a reliable improvement in the final speech-recognition task.
neurips-1992-modeling-consistency-in-a-s.tldr: Gender-conditioned speech modeling achieves accurate gender classification but no statistically significant improvement in overall recognition.

paragraphs: This paper studies neural networks as threshold circuits, whose units make decisions from weighted inputs. Circuit depth measures successive computation stages, while circuit size measures the number of gates required. The question is how quickly arithmetic can be computed in parallel without allowing the hardware requirements to grow exponentially.

The authors prove that iterated addition can be performed at depth two, and multiplication and division at depth three. Their constructions use polynomially many gates and polynomially bounded integer weights. These resource restrictions matter because the shallow computation is achieved without compensating through exponentially large circuits or weights.

Known lower bounds establish that the stated depths for these constructions are optimal. The paper contrasts threshold networks with traditional circuits built from AND, OR, and NOT gates, which face stronger depth requirements under the stated size restrictions. It also extends the techniques to depth-three powering and depth-four multiple products. The contribution is a set of mathematical constructions showing the parallel computational power of threshold gates for arithmetic.
neurips-1992-optimal-depth-neural-networ.tldr: Threshold networks compute addition, multiplication, and division at provably optimal shallow depths with polynomial resource bounds.

paragraphs: This paper addresses a mismatch between what a speech-recognition network learns to optimize and how the completed recognizer is evaluated. Its Multi-State Time Delay Neural Network uses word-level targets during training, keeping word accuracy central to both learning and testing. The motivation is to make training directly relevant to the final recognition task.

The architecture combines phoneme and word classification in a hierarchy. Dynamic time warping adjusts its connectivity pattern to accommodate temporal alignment, linking the sound-level representation to word decisions. This allows the system to incorporate timing structure while learning from targets defined at the level of recognized words.

Earlier applications emphasized small vocabularies and word spotting; this paper applies the architecture to large-vocabulary continuous speech. The authors report performance exceeding all other systems tested on the CMU Conference Registration database and describe strong performance even with limited training data. The result supports the value of maintaining consistency between the training criterion and the task-level measure used to judge the recognizer.
neurips-1992-performance-through-consist.tldr: An MS-TDNN trained directly on word-level targets achieves leading reported results on the CMU Conference Registration speech database.

paragraphs: This paper demonstrates a neural-network approach to speech synthesis organized around the physical production of speech. The model uses physiological measurements from spoken utterances to connect motor commands with articulator movement. Its intermediate representation is therefore the movement involved in producing speech, giving the synthesis process an explicit physiological stage.

The first network learns forward dynamics: how commands to muscles lead to subsequent articulator behavior. It generates movement trajectories from motor commands constrained by a phoneme input sequence and global performance parameters. This stage connects the requested speech content and overall controls to the changing configuration of the speech-producing system.

A second network takes those trajectories and generates PARCOR parameters, which are then used to synthesize the acoustic output. The two networks divide the task into learning movement dynamics and translating movement into acoustic parameters. The demonstrated paradigm shows how physiological data can support a chain from commands through articulatory motion to synthesized speech, with each learned stage handling a distinct relationship.
neurips-1992-physiologically-based-speec.tldr: Two neural networks synthesize speech by mapping motor commands to articulator movements and those movements to acoustic parameters.

paragraphs: This paper presents a method for training neural-network weights through approximate gradient descent. It estimates the gradient using finite differences, which infer the effect of a change by perturbing the system and observing the resulting difference. The goal is to obtain useful learning directions with computational and hardware requirements suited to neural implementations.

The method exploits a stochastic relationship between perturbing weights and perturbing neurons. This allows it to achieve the reported O(N³) computational complexity associated with node perturbation while avoiding access to hidden or internal neuron activity. That combination matters when internal signals are difficult to expose in a physical neural circuit.

The authors also describe the method as retaining weight perturbation's optimal hardware requirements for training VLSI neural networks. Its contribution is therefore a particular tradeoff: obtain the computational advantage of neuron-level perturbation through changes applied at the weights, without requiring internal activity measurements. The paper connects an approximation used for learning to the practical question of what information a hardware training system must access.
neurips-1992-summed-weight-neuron-pertur.tldr: A perturbation-based training method matches node perturbation's computational complexity without needing access to hidden-neuron activity.

paragraphs: This paper constructs a recurrent Elman-style network from oscillatory associative-memory modules governed by continuous differential equations. It explores how discrete symbol processing can emerge from continuous dynamics. Symbols are represented through attractors, allowing computation to proceed as transitions between stable patterns of behavior within the modules.

A rhythmic change in a bifurcation parameter supplies the machine cycle. Input and context modules are held at their attractors while hidden and output modules change state; then the latter are held while context updates for the next cycle. Learned connections coordinate these transitions, producing an architecture with discrete computational steps despite its continuous underlying dynamics.

The constructed system functions as a finite-state automaton that recognizes or generates strings defined by a Reber grammar over six symbols. The authors report better noise immunity for dynamic attractors than static ones and show that synchronization between modules matters for reliable transitions. The work connects grammar processing to a concrete dynamical mechanism in which oscillation, timing, and coordination contribute to computation.
neurips-1992-synchronization-and-grammat.tldr: Clocked oscillatory memory modules implement an Elman-style grammar processor whose reliable transitions depend on attractors and synchronization.

paragraphs: This paper analyzes stochastic learning by treating network weights as random variables. Instead of describing just one sequence of weight updates, it follows a probability density over possible weight configurations. The density evolves through a Markov process, providing a way to study the changing distribution of learning outcomes over time.

The authors summarize the evolution theory and illustrate how stochastic learning differs from batch gradient descent. This perspective addresses the search process itself, including transient behavior before settling near an optimum. It also makes it possible to examine movement between basins, the regions associated with different optima in weight space.

Using the formalism, the paper predicts how long noise takes to drive a network from one basin to another. Those predictions are compared with simulations of large ensembles of networks on simple supervised and unsupervised problems. The contribution is a framework for studying where learning travels and how long transitions take, extending the analysis beyond whether a learning procedure eventually converges.
neurips-1992-weight-space-probability-de.tldr: A probability-density view of stochastic learning predicts transient behavior and noise-driven transition times between different optima.
